## Background

All functions in R have at least 3 things:

- a *name* (we pick this and use it to call the function)
- input *arguments* (one or more comma separated inputs)
- the *body*(the lines of R code that do the work of the function)

## A first function

Let's write a function to add some numbers

```{r}
add <- function(x, y=0, z=0) {
  x + y + z
}
```

We can test it out

```{r}
add(1, 100)
add(c(1, 2, 10), 100)
add(100)
```

Function arguments can be *required* or *optional*. This just means they have a default fall back value that is used if the user does not supply one (like our `y` input above).

What if I wanted to run our `add()` function in three inputs.

```{r}
add(1, 100, 1)
```

**Side-note**: R has the ability to take any number of inputs that you don't have to spell out like our `x`, `y` and `z` via `...` called "dots" or "elipses" input argument.

We can explicitly output or **return** a value from a function with the special function `return()`. It is often a good idea to use this even though we might not need it.

## A DNA sequence generator

Write a function to generate random nucleotide sequences and the user can specify the length of the sequence you want.

A useful function to get us started here is the base R `sample()` function.

```{r}
sample(x= c("A", "C", "T", "G"), size=40, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.30, .20, .30, .20))
```

This is our working "snippet" of code that does what we want so lets make it a function.

```{r}
generate_dna <- function(seqlength=25){
  sample(x= c("A", "C", "T", "G"), size=seqlength, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.30, .20, .30, .20))
}
```

```{r}
generate_dna(30)
```

### Optional format switch

At the minute our function returns sequences like this "A" "T" "A" "C" "T" "G" "T" "T" i.e. a multi element character vector with one nucleotide per element of the vector.

We may want it to look like this ATACTGTT which will likely be more useful.

A base R function that might help us here is `paste()`

```{r}
paste(c("A", "C", "T", "G"), collapse = "")
```

```{r}
generate_dna <- function(seqlength=25){
  n <- sample(x= c("A", "C", "T", "G"), size=seqlength, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.30, .20, .30, .20))
  paste(n, collapse = "")
}

generate_dna(30)
```

We want to allow the user to pick the format, for this we can use a TRUE/FALSE kind of input argument...

```{r}
generate_dna <- function(seqlength=25, fasta = TRUE){
  n <- sample(x= c("A", "C", "T", "G"), size=seqlength, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.30, .20, .30, .20))
  cat("Hello...")
 if(fasta) {
   cat("...is it me you're looking for...")
   n <- paste(n, collapse = "")
 }
  return(n)
}
generate_dna(30)
```

```{r}
x <- generate_dna(30, fasta=TRUE)
x
```

The `return()` function will explicitly print things.

```{r}
generate_dna <- function(seqlength=25, fasta = TRUE){
  n <- sample(x= c("A", "C", "T", "G"), size=seqlength, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.30, .20, .30, .20))
 if(fasta) {
   n <- paste(n, collapse = "")
 }
  cat(n)
}
generate_dna(6, fasta=TRUE)
```

We want FASTA format like te rest of the world uses

> len6 AGTCAT

```{r}
generate_dna <- function(seqlength=25, fasta = TRUE){
  n <- sample(x= c("A", "C", "T", "G"), size=seqlength, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.30, .20, .30, .20))
 if(fasta) {
   id <- paste(">len", seqlength, sep="")
   n <- paste(n, collapse = "")
   cat(id,sep="\n", n)
 }
  return(n)
}

```

```{r}
x <- generate_dna(10)
```

## A Protein Generator

> Q. Write a function called `generate_protein()` that makes random peptide sequences.

```{r}
generate_protein <- function(seqlength=15, fasta = TRUE){
  
  aa <- c("A", "R", "N", "D", "C", "Q", "E", "G", "H", "I", "L", "K", "M", "F", "P", "S", "T", "W", "Y", "V") 
  n <- sample(aa, size=seqlength, replace = TRUE)
  if(fasta) {
    id <- paste(">len", seqlength, sep="")
   n <- paste(n, collapse = "")
   
   cat(id,sep="\n", n)
  }
  return(n)
}
```

```{r}
p <- generate_protein(30)
```

> Q. Use our new `generate_protein()` function to make a series of random protein sequences ranging from 6 to 13 amino acids in length

```{r}
for (i in 6:13) {
  x <- generate_protein(i)
}
```

Another very R specific way to do this is with the `sapply()` function:

```{r}
fasta_list <- sapply(6:13, generate_protein)
```

> Q. Are these sequences unique in nature? To test this we will BLASTp all of them against the NR database.

| Length | %Cov | %Iden | Unique |
|--------|------|-------|--------|
| 6      | 100  | 100   | No     |
| 7      | 100  | 100   | No     |
| 8      | 88   | 100   | Yes    |
| 9      | 89   | 100   | Yes    |
| 10     | 90   | 90    | Yes    |
| 11     | 100  | 78.57 | Yes    |

The connection to immunology is that the peptides that are normally presented on immune cells are 8-9 amino acids long and that is around the minimum length where sequences start to be unique.
